extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in U.S. constitutional theory and the design of representative government
extracted.subtask_description: James Madison's argument about structuring the House of Representatives: who may vote, who may serve, appropriate term length and frequency of elections, and the institutional checks that secure dependence on the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of electors set by state standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those of the former are to be the same with those of the electors of the most numerous branch of the State Legislatures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the definition of the right of suffrage as a fundamental article of republican government; use the standard already established in each State (the electors of the most numerous branch of the State Legislatures) rather than leaving the rule to occasional Congressional regulation or to varying State legislative discretion. This preserves conformity with local standards and prevents undue dependence of the federal branch on state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix suffrage in the Constitution (do not leave to Congress or States)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was incumbent on the Convention, therefore, to define and establish this right in the Constitution. To have left it open for the occasional regulation of the Congress, would have been improper... To have submitted it to the Legislative discretion of the States, would have been improper for the same reason..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right of suffrage should be established in the federal Constitution to prevent it being altered by ordinary legislative action (either federal or state) in ways that could impair republican principles or make a federal branch dependent on state governments. Fixing suffrage protects against temporary or partisan changes that would abridge rights secured by the federal Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing a single uniform suffrage rule across States
rubrics_metrics.description: "To have reduced the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule, would probably have been as dissatisfactory to some of the States, as it would have been difficult to the Convention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single uniform national qualification for electors was judged impractical and likely to upset some States; using existing state standards is the practical compromise that respects state diversity while securing federal safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for Representatives (eligibility requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative must be at least twenty-five years old; must have been seven years a citizen of the United States; must, at the time of his election, be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent; and, during the time of his service, must be in no office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the concrete, enumerated eligibility criteria for service in the House. They are presented as reasonable limitations intended to allow open access while ensuring minimal ties/commitments that would conflict with representative duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of access to office (non-discriminatory eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under these reasonable limitations, the door of this part of the Federal Government is open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, whether young or old, and without regard to poverty or wealth, or to any particular profession of religious faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility rules are intended to be non-discriminatory with respect to birthplace, age (beyond minimum), economic status, profession, or religion, so that merit rather than social or economic status determines access to the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections secure dependence and sympathy with the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "As it is essential to liberty, that the Government in general should have a common interest with the People; so it is particularly essential, that the branch of it under consideration should have an immediate dependence on, and an intimate sympathy with the People. Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectually secured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections must be frequent enough to keep Representatives responsive to popular interests; the precise optimal frequency depends on context, but the principle is that frequent popular renewal binds Representatives to constituents and preserves liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial elections are appropriate for the House
rubrics_metrics.description: Madison argues that biennial elections "cannot possibly be dangerous to the requisite dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using historical comparisons (British triennial/septennial practices, Irish octennial/parliamentary abuses, colonial variations from one to seven years, and Virginia's septennial example), Madison concludes biennial elections under the federal scheme strike a proper balance: frequent enough to secure dependence, but not impracticably frequent. The page uses these precedents as empirical support for biennial terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/empirical examples to judge election frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Madison consults examples (House of Commons in Great Britain, Irish Parliament, colonial state practices) to assess what election frequencies have secured dependence and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding term lengths, evaluate historical regimes with analogous features and consider how frequency affected representatives' dependence on the people. The guidance includes rejecting overly vague comparisons and preferring the best-known analogous examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: greater power requires shorter duration
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a received and well-founded maxim, that where no other circumstances affect the case, the greater the power is, the shorter ought to be its duration; and conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely may its duration be protracted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the magnitude of delegated authority as a rule for setting term lengths: bodies with greater substantive power should be subject to more frequent electoral check; less powerful bodies may safely have longer terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks by collateral (state) legislatures limit federal representatives' abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Madison notes the Federal Legislature "will be moreover watched and controlled by the several collateral Legislatures," which provides an additional restraint not present in more centralized legislatures like the British Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional constraints from multiple legislatures (state bodies) are counted as part of the design: because state legislatures will provide oversight and competition of authority, the House is less likely to be seduced or abused, allowing somewhat longer terms than a wholly dominant parliament might have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative limitation of federal legislative power vs. British Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Legislature will possess a part only of that supreme Legislative authority which is vested completely in the British Parliament; ... With less power, therefore, the Federal Representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating appropriate institutional design, account for the comparative share of power: because the federal legislature will not concentrate the broad powers of the British Parliament, considerations about term length and safeguards differ; lesser centralized power reduces the risk from longer durations.
